units.t: Mission, vision, stakeholders & the strategy process
Levels of strategy & how firms compete
Internal analysis: value chain, VRIO, BCG
External analysis: SWOT, PESTEL, Porter's 5 forces
How strategies emerge: intended vs realized
Goals, MBO, Balanced Scorecard, SMART, KPI, CSR
Lewin's three stages & Kotter's eight steps
Schein's culture change & comparing the models

questions.q: A manager studies customer complaints and industry reports to identify developments that may affect the organization. Which Mintzberg managerial role is illustrated?
o: Monitor
Resource allocator
Leader
Negotiator
questions.x: Studying complaints, reports and trends = collecting information, so the monitor role (informational).

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the view that management is “the art of getting things done through the efforts of other people”?
o: Managers achieve objectives by coordinating and supporting the work of others.
Managers are responsible only for measuring employee performance.
Managers contribute mainly by creating formal rules and procedures.
Managers should personally complete the organization's most important tasks.
questions.x: Management = reaching goals through other people, so coordinating and supporting their work.

questions.q: What is organizational commitment?
o: Emotional attachment to the company
Our pay level
A job task list
Compliance with organizational rules and policies
questions.x: Organizational commitment = the emotional attachment people have to the company they work for.

questions.q: Which is a key job attitude at work?
o: Charisma
Job characteristics
Personality
Job satisfaction
questions.x: The two key work attitudes are job satisfaction and organizational commitment. Personality and charisma are traits; job characteristics are causes of attitudes.

questions.q: Which decision type sets the organization’s course?
o: Strategic
Tactical
Operational
Programmed
questions.x: Strategic decisions set the organization's long-term course; tactical and operational decisions implement it.

questions.q: Which is a nonverbal communication cue?
o: Facial expressions
Memo
Phone call
Text
questions.x: Facial expressions are nonverbal. Memos, texts and phone calls use words (verbal or written).

questions.q: A manufacturer is replacing a polluting production process with cleaner technology. The operations director defines conversion targets, assigns responsibilities, and monitors deadlines. She also invites employees from different backgrounds and job levels to discuss how the change may affect them and adapt the training accordingly. Which description best summarizes the director’s leadership behavior?
o: Task-oriented and people-oriented leadership balancing targets with employee inclusion
Task-oriented and autocratic leadership emphasizing targets and centralized managerial control
People-oriented and democratic leadership emphasizing consultation without formal performance targets
Laissez-faire and people-oriented leadership allowing employees to direct implementation independently
questions.x: Targets, responsibilities and deadlines = task-oriented. Inviting employees and adapting training = people-oriented. She does both.

questions.q: An international energy crisis sharply increases operating costs. A hotel CEO offers managers short-term rewards for meeting immediate energy-saving targets. At the same time, she communicates a longer-term vision of transforming the hotel group into a climate-neutral business and encourages experimentation with new technologies. Which pair of leadership approaches is demonstrated by the CEO?
o: Laissez-faire leadership for short-term targets and autocratic leadership for long-term change
Ethical leadership for short-term targets and charismatic leadership for long-term change
Servant leadership for short-term targets and authentic leadership for long-term change
Transactional leadership for short-term targets and transformational leadership for long-term change
questions.x: Short-term rewards for hitting targets = transactional (contingent reward). A long-term vision plus encouraging experimentation = transformational.

questions.q: In a PESTEL analysis, the planned reduction of government solar subsidies is primarily which factor?
o: An economic factor involving household income and changing consumer purchasing power; this classification clarifies which external force is shaping the organization's strategic environment.

A social factor involving household preferences and community attitudes toward renewable energy; this classification clarifies which external force is shaping the organization's strategic environment.
A political factor involving priorities and public support for solar adoption; this classification clarifies which external force is shaping the organization's strategic environment
A technological factor involving battery performance and digital energy-management systems; this classification clarifies which external force is shaping the organization's strategic environment.
A legal factor involving binding court judgments and contractual disputes with customers; this classification clarifies which external force is shaping the organization's strategic environment.
An environmental factor involving emissions targets and the physical effects of climate change; this classification clarifies which external force is shaping the organization's strategic environment.
questions.x: Subsidies are a government policy choice, so a political factor. A binding law or court ruling would be legal.

questions.q: Which function of management focuses on defining goals and determining how to achieve them?
o: Organizing
Controlling
Planning
Leading
questions.x: Planning = setting goals and deciding how to reach them.

questions.q: A department manager compares actual monthly expenses with the approved budget and investigates significant differences. Which management function is the manager performing?
o: Controlling
Organizing
Planning
Leading
questions.x: Comparing actual performance with a standard and investigating the differences = controlling.

questions.q: An employee consistently prepares carefully, meets deadlines, and follows through on commitments. What work attitude is predominant?
o: Organizational Commitment
Agreeableness
Extraversion
Openness to experience
questions.x: Careful, punctual and reliable is the trait conscientiousness, which is not an option here. The question asks for a work attitude, and organizational commitment is the only work attitude listed; the other three are Big Five traits. Read 'attitude' versus 'trait' carefully.

questions.q: Which job characteristic links to satisfaction?
o: Stress
Autonomy at work
Organizational justice
Personality
questions.x: Autonomy is a job characteristic (with skill variety, feedback and task significance). Justice and stress are other causes of attitudes, and personality is not a feature of the job.

questions.q: A manager must communicate a sensitive restructuring decision, answer employees’ questions, and observe their reactions immediately. Which communication channel is most appropriate?
o: A standard monthly report
A notice on the staff portal
A prerecorded audio message
A face-to-face meeting
questions.x: A sensitive message where you must answer questions and see reactions needs the richest channel: face to face.

questions.q: Before presenting a proposal, a manager converts her ideas into words, diagrams, and numerical tables. Which part of the communication process is this?
o: Encoding
Filtering
Decoding
Feedback
questions.x: Turning ideas into words, diagrams and numbers = encoding.

questions.q: Which goal best satisfies the SMART criteria?
o: Improve customer service significantly.
Encourage employees to respond to customers more quickly.
Become the industry's most respected company.
Reduce average customer waiting time from eight to five minutes by 30 June.
questions.x: Only this goal is specific, measurable (8 → 5 minutes) and time-bound (by 30 June).

questions.q: What is a goal?
o: An outcome statement of what to accomplish
A time-based measurable action
A detailed strategy plan
A company's mission statement
questions.x: A goal is an outcome statement of what you want to accomplish. An objective is the precise, time-based, measurable action.

questions.q: A company enters a foreign market by creating a new business that it owns together with a local company. Which global expansion strategy is this?
o: Wholly owned subsidiary
Exporting
Joint venture
Licensing
questions.x: A new business owned together with a local firm = joint venture.

questions.q: In a strongly collectivist culture, which managerial practice is most likely to be effective?
o: Avoiding long-term relationships among team members
Emphasizing only individual competition and personal recognition
Assigning work without considering group membership
Connecting rewards and goals to the performance of the group
questions.x: Collectivist cultures put the group first, so tie rewards and goals to group performance.

questions.q: A cybersecurity specialist influences an executive team because of her knowledge and experience, although she has no formal managerial position. Which source of power explains her influence?
o: Reward power
Coercive power
Legitimate power
Expert power
questions.x: Influence from knowledge and experience without a formal position = expert power.

questions.q: A company enters a country where unofficial payments are commonly used to speed up permits. Although competitors follow this practice, the regional director refuses to authorize such payments. She openly explains that the company’s anti-corruption principles apply in every market, even if expansion becomes slower. Which pair of leadership approaches is demonstrated by the director?
o: Transactional and charismatic leadership emphasizing exchange and personal influence
Servant and transformational leadership emphasizing employee development and organizational vision
Laissez-faire and autocratic leadership emphasizing independence and centralized authority
Ethical and authentic leadership emphasizing integrity and consistency with stated principles
questions.x: Refusing bribes even at a cost = ethical leadership. Openly acting consistently with stated principles in every market = authentic leadership.

questions.q: A manager discovers that a highly profitable supplier uses unsafe working conditions. She ends the contract despite the short-term financial cost because the supplier’s conduct conflicts with the organization’s stated principles. What most clearly guides her decision?
o: Values-based leadership
Laissez-faire leadership
Management by exception
Coercive leadership
questions.x: Ending the contract because it conflicts with the organization's stated principles = values-based leadership.

questions.q: An electronics company creates teams to design energy-efficient products for customers with different physical abilities. Engineers remain members of specialist departments but also report to product managers. Each team includes employees with varied professional, cultural, and personal backgrounds. Which combination of organizational concepts appears in the case?
o: Matrix structure with dual reporting and a professionally diverse product team
Geographic structure with regional authority and a culturally uniform product team
Virtual structure with remote coordination and a geographically uniform product team
Functional structure with specialization and a professionally uniform product team
questions.x: Reporting to a specialist department and a product manager at once = matrix (dual reporting). Varied backgrounds = a diverse team.

questions.q: A consumer-goods company forms a team to reduce plastic packaging. Members come from engineering, marketing, logistics, and several cultural backgrounds. The leader establishes inclusive discussion rules and ensures that each member’s expertise is considered before decisions are made. Which interpretation best explains the value of the team’s approach?
o: Similar cultural experience increases agreement, while informal norms reduce competing viewpoints
Shared professional knowledge increases consistency, while majority voting limits extended discussion
Diverse member knowledge increases alternatives, while inclusive norms support constructive discussion
Centralized leader knowledge increases speed, while fixed procedures reduce alternative proposals
questions.x: Diverse knowledge gives more alternatives; inclusive discussion rules keep the debate constructive (and prevent groupthink).

questions.q: Which option correctly interprets the hospitals’ price negotiations using Porter’s Five Forces?
o: Competitive rivalry because rural patients can negotiate directly over MedLink's institutional contract prices; this interpretation clarifies how customer concentration influences competitive pressure and negotiation outcomes.

Threat of substitutes because teaching hospitals can influence data-protection rules across national markets; this interpretation clarifies how customer concentration influences competitive pressure and negotiation outcomes.

Complementor power because medical regulators can replace hospitals as the platform's principal customers; this interpretation clarifies how customer concentration influences competitive pressure and negotiation outcomes.

Threat of entrants because existing hospital customers can create mandatory cybersecurity standards; this interpretation clarifies how customer concentration influences competitive pressure and negotiation outcomes.

Supplier power because software developers can determine the prices hospitals pay for consultations; this interpretation clarifies how customer concentration influences competitive pressure and negotiation outcomes.

Buyer power because major hospital customers can pressure MedLink during contract negotiations; this interpretation clarifies how customer concentration influences competitive pressure and negotiation outcomes.
questions.x: A few large hospital groups buy most subscriptions, so they can push on price: bargaining power of buyers.

questions.q: The cybersecurity department’s detailed plan for implementing stronger data protection is which strategy level?
o: Stakeholder strategy because it only classifies hospitals according to their relative power and interest; this classification connects departmental priorities with the organization's broader strategic direction and competitive approach.

Realized strategy because it necessarily emerges without management planning or formal organizational approval; this classification connects departmental priorities with the organization's broader strategic direction and competitive approach

Corporate strategy because it determines the countries and industries in which MedLink will operate; this classification connects departmental priorities with the organization's broader strategic direction and competitive approach.

Divisional strategy because it decides whether MedLink should acquire unrelated healthcare companies; this classification connects departmental priorities with the organization's broader strategic direction and competitive approach.

Business strategy because it establishes the platform's overall competitive position against market rivals; this classification connects departmental priorities with the organization's broader strategic direction and competitive approach.

Functional strategy because it translates broader priorities into departmental actions and procedures; this classification connects departmental priorities with the organization's broader strategic direction and competitive approach.
questions.x: A department translating broader priorities into its own actions and procedures = functional strategy.

questions.q: Which PESTEL combination best captures the new privacy rules and improving telehealth technology?
o: Social and environmental factors involving patient expectations and the physical effects of climate change; this interpretation separates regulatory obligations from technological developments affecting the organization's future direction.

Environmental and social factors involving resource use and public attitudes toward remote consultations; this interpretation separates regulatory obligations from technological developments affecting the organization's future direction.

Economic and political factors involving inflation rates and government healthcare spending priorities; this interpretation separates regulatory obligations from technological developments affecting the organization's future direction.

Legal and technological factors involving data obligations and advances in digital healthcare systems; this interpretation separates regulatory obligations from technological developments affecting the organization's future direction

Political and economic factors involving government stability and changing healthcare purchasing power; this interpretation separates regulatory obligations from technological developments affecting the organization's future direction.

Technological and economic factors involving software development and hospital budget limitations only; this interpretation separates regulatory obligations from technological developments affecting the organization's future direction.
questions.x: Privacy legislation = legal. Better encryption, video and integration = technological.

questions.q: Which action in the case most clearly represents Lewin’s unfreezing stage?
o: Standardizing the tested workflow and documenting it as the permanent assembly procedure; this interpretation identifies the stage concerned with creating readiness before new behavior is introduced.
Explaining competitive threats and showing why existing production practices must change; this interpretation identifies the stage concerned with creating readiness before new behavior is introduced

Embedding robot-related responsibilities in job descriptions and formal performance-management systems; this interpretation identifies the stage concerned with creating readiness before new behavior is introduced.

Measuring long-term performance after the technology has become part of normal operations; this interpretation identifies the stage concerned with creating readiness before new behavior is introduced.

Installing robots across every production line after the pilot has demonstrated stable results; this interpretation identifies the stage concerned with creating readiness before new behavior is introduced.

Rewarding employees who consistently use the finalized robotic assembly procedures correctly; this interpretation identifies the stage concerned with creating readiness before new behavior is introduced.
questions.x: Unfreezing creates readiness: showing the competitive threat and why the current way can't continue.

questions.q: Employees who openly organize protests against the robots are demonstrating which reaction to change?
o: Enthusiastic support because they publicly promote the new technology and encourage participation; this classification explains the visibility and intensity of employees' response to the proposed organizational change.

Compliance because they follow instructions despite having personal doubts about the technology; this classification explains the visibility and intensity of employees' response to the proposed organizational change.

Passive acceptance because they privately support the change without becoming actively involved; this classification explains the visibility and intensity of employees' response to the proposed organizational change.

Passive resistance because they quietly delay work while avoiding any visible opposition; this classification explains the visibility and intensity of employees' response to the proposed organizational change.

Commitment because they personally invest effort in ensuring the change succeeds over time; this classification explains the visibility and intensity of employees' response to the proposed organizational change.

Active resistance because they openly challenge and organize opposition to the planned change; this classification explains the visibility and intensity of employees' response to the proposed organizational change.
questions.x: Open, visible and organized opposition = active resistance.

questions.q: Which option best explains a practice associated with an innovative culture at HarborTech?
o: Restricting improvement ideas to senior managers with formal authority over manufacturing decisions; this interpretation shows how leadership practices can encourage responsible experimentation and organizational learning.

Punishing unsuccessful experiments even when teams follow agreed learning and safety procedures; this interpretation shows how leadership practices can encourage responsible experimentation and organizational learning.

Evaluating employees only on short-term output and excluding learning from performance discussions; this interpretation shows how leadership practices can encourage responsible experimentation and organizational learning.

Preventing cross-functional communication so departments can protect their specialized operational knowledge; this interpretation shows how leadership practices can encourage responsible experimentation and organizational learning.

Requiring teams to preserve existing methods until competitors have proven every new technology; this interpretation shows how leadership practices can encourage responsible experimentation and organizational learning.

Supporting safe experiments, sharing lessons, and recognizing employees who propose responsible improvements; this interpretation shows how leadership practices can encourage responsible experimentation and organizational learning
questions.x: Innovative cultures support safe experiments, share lessons and reward responsible ideas instead of punishing failure.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the view that management is “the art of getting things done through the efforts of other people”?
o: Managers contribute mainly by creating formal rules and procedures.
Managers should personally complete the organization's most important tasks.
Managers are responsible only for measuring employee performance.
Managers achieve objectives by coordinating and supporting the work of others.
questions.x: Management = reaching goals through other people, so coordinating and supporting their work.

questions.q: Which function of management focuses on defining goals and determining how to achieve them?
o: Planning
Organizing
Controlling
Leading
questions.x: Planning = setting goals and deciding how to reach them.

questions.q: A manager redesigns the department by grouping related tasks and assigning responsibility for each group to a team leader. Which management function does this best illustrate?
o: Leading
Organizing
Controlling
Forecasting
questions.x: Grouping tasks and assigning responsibility = designing structure, so organizing.

questions.q: A manager studies customer complaints and industry reports to identify developments that may affect the organization. Which Mintzberg managerial role is illustrated?
o: Negotiator
Monitor
Leader
Resource allocator
questions.x: Studying complaints, reports and trends = collecting information, so the monitor role (informational).

questions.q: What is organizational commitment?
o: Our pay level
A job task list
Compliance with organizational rules and policies
Emotional attachment to the company
questions.x: Organizational commitment = the emotional attachment people have to the company they work for.

questions.q: Which is a key job attitude at work?
o: Job satisfaction
Charisma
Personality
Job characteristics
questions.x: The two key work attitudes are job satisfaction and organizational commitment. Personality and charisma are traits; job characteristics are causes of attitudes.

questions.q: What does an attitude refer to?
o: Our pay and benefits
A plan we make
A learned ability to perform a task
Our opinions, beliefs, and feelings about our environment
questions.x: An attitude = our opinions, beliefs and feelings about aspects of our environment.

questions.q: An employee consistently prepares carefully, meets deadlines, and follows through on commitments. What work attitude is predominant?
o: Organizational Commitment
Extraversion
Openness to experience
Agreeableness
questions.x: Careful, punctual and reliable is the trait conscientiousness, which is not an option here. The question asks for a work attitude, and organizational commitment is the only work attitude listed; the other three are Big Five traits. Read 'attitude' versus 'trait' carefully.

questions.q: Two employees heard the same announcement. One interprets it as an opportunity, while the other interprets it as a threat because of previous experiences. Which communication barrier best explains the difference?
o: Formalization
Channel expansion
Upward communication
Selective perception
questions.x: Interpreting the same message differently because of your own experiences and expectations = selective perception.

questions.q: Which decision-making model aims for a “satisfactory” outcome?
o: Intuitive
Creative
Rational
Bounded rationality
questions.x: Bounded rationality leads to satisficing: choosing the first alternative that meets your minimum criteria.

questions.q: Which is a nonverbal communication cue?
o: Text
Phone call
Facial expressions
Memo
questions.x: Facial expressions are nonverbal. Memos, texts and phone calls use words (verbal or written).

questions.q: Which is a component of the communication process?
o: Filtering
Strategic decision
Message
Creativity
questions.x: The message is part of the process (sender, message, channel, receiver, noise, feedback). Filtering is a barrier.

questions.q: A restaurant automatically reorders a standard quantity of ingredients whenever inventory reaches a predetermined level. What type of decision is this?
o: Creative decision
Strategic decision
Nonprogrammed decision
Programmed decision
questions.x: A routine, recurring decision handled by a fixed rule = programmed decision.

questions.q: What is a goal?
o: A time-based measurable action
A company's mission statement
An outcome statement of what to accomplish
A detailed strategy plan
questions.x: A goal is an outcome statement of what you want to accomplish. An objective is the precise, time-based, measurable action.

questions.q: What does Management by Objectives (MBO) aim to do?
o: Define the company mission and vision
Align subordinate objectives with overall goals
Translate mission into measures
Report on social and environmental results
questions.x: MBO (Drucker) aligns employees' objectives with the organization's overall goals.

questions.q: What does the Balanced Scorecard do?
o: Lists only financial targets for the year
Sets individual pay levels
Turns mission and strategy into measurable goals and tracks them
Describes values for employee behavior
questions.x: It translates mission and strategy into measurable goals in four perspectives and tracks them.

questions.q: An employee believes that she contributes more effort than a colleague but receives the same reward. She responds by reducing her effort. Which motivation theory best explains her response?
o: Reinforcement theory
ERG theory
Equity theory
Maslow's hierarchy of needs
questions.x: Comparing your effort/reward ratio with a colleague and restoring fairness by working less = equity theory.

questions.q: What is an objective?
o: A precise, time-based, measurable action
A broad vision of success
A long-term goal that defines direction of the organization
A general outcome statement
questions.x: An objective is precise, time-based and measurable. The broad outcome statement is a goal.

questions.q: A national culture strongly values cooperation, quality of life, and concern for others rather than competition and visible achievement. In Hofstede’s framework, this culture is relatively:
o: Feminine
High in uncertainty avoidance
Masculine
High in power distance
questions.x: Valuing cooperation and quality of life over competition and achievement = a feminine culture (low masculinity).

questions.q: According to Hofstede’s Cultural Framework, what is meant by “uncertainty avoidance”?
o: The preference for long-term planning and perseverance over short-term outcomes.
Trade between regions.
The preference for local markets.
The degree to which people in a society feel comfortable with risk and ambiguity.
questions.x: Uncertainty avoidance = how comfortable people in a society are with risk and ambiguity.

questions.q: What is “power distance” in Hofstede’s model?
o: Acceptance of power and authority differences
Preference for collective interests over individual ones
Focus on risk and uncertainty
Value of work and earnings
questions.x: Power distance = how much people accept unequal distribution of power and authority.

questions.q: A culture emphasizes persistence, future rewards, and future investment rather than immediate results. Which Hofstede dimension does this describe?
o: Long-term orientation
Power distance
Masculinity
Individualism
questions.x: Persistence and future rewards over immediate results = long-term orientation.

questions.q: Employees accept a newly appointed director’s instructions because the director has formal authority over the department. Which source of power is being used?
o: Legitimate power
Coercive power
Expert power
Referent power
questions.x: Following instructions because of formal authority = legitimate power.

questions.q: A design manager notices that senior employees dominate meetings while younger colleagues and employees with disabilities rarely contribute. She introduces structured speaking turns, asks quieter members for input, and uses their suggestions to improve product accessibility. Team members increasingly respect her commitment to inclusion. Which description best explains the manager’s approach and influence?
o: Task-oriented leadership and coercive power based on targets and possible sanctions
Laissez-faire leadership and legitimate power based on independence and formal position
People-oriented leadership and referent power based on inclusion and earned respect
Autocratic leadership and reward power based on centralized decisions and incentives
questions.x: Drawing out quieter members and including them = people-oriented. The respect she earns from that = referent power.

questions.q: A company enters a country where unofficial payments are commonly used to speed up permits. Although competitors follow this practice, the regional director refuses to authorize such payments. She openly explains that the company’s anti-corruption principles apply in every market, even if expansion becomes slower. Which pair of leadership approaches is demonstrated by the director?
o: Servant and transformational leadership emphasizing employee development and organizational vision
Transactional and charismatic leadership emphasizing exchange and personal influence
Laissez-faire and autocratic leadership emphasizing independence and centralized authority
Ethical and authentic leadership emphasizing integrity and consistency with stated principles
questions.x: Refusing bribes even at a cost = ethical leadership. Openly acting consistently with stated principles in every market = authentic leadership.

questions.q: A manager discovers that a highly profitable supplier uses unsafe working conditions. She ends the contract despite the short-term financial cost because the supplier’s conduct conflicts with the organization’s stated principles. What most clearly guides her decision?
o: Coercive leadership
Laissez-faire leadership
Values-based leadership
Management by exception
questions.x: Ending the contract because it conflicts with the organization's stated principles = values-based leadership.

questions.q: An electronics company creates teams to design energy-efficient products for customers with different physical abilities. Engineers remain members of specialist departments but also report to product managers. Each team includes employees with varied professional, cultural, and personal backgrounds. Which combination of organizational concepts appears in the case?
o: Functional structure with specialization and a professionally uniform product team
Geographic structure with regional authority and a culturally uniform product team
Virtual structure with remote coordination and a geographically uniform product team
Matrix structure with dual reporting and a professionally diverse product team
questions.x: Reporting to a specialist department and a product manager at once = matrix (dual reporting). Varied backgrounds = a diverse team.

questions.q: A food company operates in regions facing different climate risks and environmental rules. It reorganizes its operations into geographic divisions so that the managers can adapt sourcing, products, and sustainability practices to local conditions. Which interpretation best explains the organizational change?
o: Internal technological pressures encourage a matrix structure tailored to temporary projects
Internal cultural pressures encourage a functional structure tailored to specialist occupations
External competitive pressures encourage a divisional structure tailored to separate product lines
External natural and legal pressures encourage a geographic structure tailored to regional conditions
questions.x: Climate risks (natural) and environmental rules (legal) are external pressures; reorganizing by region = geographic structure.

questions.q: A travel company plans sustainable services for a rapidly growing international market. Its project team includes members with different cultural backgrounds and professional expertise. The team also consults local community leaders, environmental experts, and industry partners to understand emerging expectations and opportunities. Which interpretation best explains the factors strengthening the response?
o: Team diversity broadens market insight, while strategic networking identifies future trends and opportunities
Centralized expertise broadens international insight, while closed networking identifies future partnership opportunities
Cultural similarity broadens sustainability insight, while personal networking identifies future regulatory developments
Professional similarity broadens customer insight, while operational networking identifies future market developments
questions.x: Diverse members broaden insight; consulting outside leaders and experts about future trends = strategic networking.

questions.q: A shift toward hybrid work leads a company to add remote specialists from several countries to an established product team. The team leader notices uncertainty about roles, technology, and meeting expectations. She schedules orientation sessions and helps members rebuild shared working agreements. Which two team-development stages best match the change described?
o: Storming after adding members, followed by performing after the first orientation session
Norming after adding members, followed by adjourning after agreements are established
Performing after adding members, followed by storming as role expectations become clear
Forming after adding members, followed by norming as shared agreements develop
questions.x: New members restart the team at forming (uncertainty about roles); rebuilding shared working agreements = norming.

questions.q: Which option correctly classifies FreshLoop’s focus on durability, convenience, and patented freshness technology?
o: Retrenchment based on reducing services, closing collection points, and limiting customer availability; this classification explains the basis on which the company intends to compete in its market.
Unrelated diversification based on entering industries with no connection to reusable food packaging; this classification explains the basis on which the company intends to compete in its market.

Differentiation based on distinctive durability, convenience, and food-preservation benefits for customers; this classification explains the basis on which the company intends to compete in its market
Vertical divestment based on selling the patented technology and outsourcing every customer interaction; this classification explains the basis on which the company intends to compete in its market.
Cost leadership based on offering standardized containers at the lowest possible market price; this classification explains the basis on which the company intends to compete in its market.
Market withdrawal based on leaving existing customers and ending all deposit-return activities; this classification explains the basis on which the company intends to compete in its market.
questions.x: Competing on unique durability, convenience and patented technology = differentiation.

questions.q: How should FreshLoop’s shift from retailer subscriptions to deposit-return services be classified?
o: An intended strategy because it was fully planned before the customer pilots began; this classification explains how experience changed the strategy that the organization actually followed

A corporate mission because it defines the organization's fundamental purpose and principal stakeholders; this classification explains how experience changed the strategy that the organization actually followed.
A realized strategy because it emerged from experience and differed from the original plan; this classification explains how experience changed the strategy that the organization actually followed
A stakeholder map because it classifies external groups according to power and interest; this classification explains how experience changed the strategy that the organization actually followed.

A functional strategy because it concerns only one department's routine operational responsibilities; this classification explains how experience changed the strategy that the organization actually followed.

A vision statement because it describes the company's preferred position in the distant future; this classification explains how experience changed the strategy that the organization actually followed.
questions.x: The pattern that emerged from the pilots and differed from the original plan = realized (emergent) strategy.

questions.q: Which value-chain activity is most directly represented by FreshLoop’s collection points and cleaning hubs?
o: Firm infrastructure involving governance, financial control, legal support, and strategic planning processes; this interpretation shows where the activity contributes directly or indirectly to customer value.
Operations involving the collection, cleaning, preparation, and recirculation of reusable containers; this interpretation shows where the activity contributes directly or indirectly to customer value

Human-resource management involving recruitment, training, compensation, and development of company employees; this interpretation shows where the activity contributes directly or indirectly to customer value.
Marketing and sales involving customer communication, pricing, promotion, and contract development; this interpretation shows where the activity contributes directly or indirectly to customer value.

Technology development involving research, product design, and improvement of the patented sealing system; this interpretation shows where the activity contributes directly or indirectly to customer value.
Procurement involving the selection and purchase of raw materials from approved external suppliers; this interpretation shows where the activity contributes directly or indirectly to customer value.
questions.x: Collecting, cleaning and recirculating containers directly produces the service = operations, a primary activity.

questions.q: Which Kotter step is represented by presenting waiting-time data and citizen complaints?
o: Building a coalition by selecting influential people who can guide the change together; this classification identifies the early change step that challenges complacency and establishes a reason for action.

Enlisting volunteers by encouraging a broad group of employees to support implementation; this classification identifies the early change step that challenges complacency and establishes a reason for action.

Forming a vision by describing the desired future of accessible municipal permit services; this classification identifies the early change step that challenges complacency and establishes a reason for action.

Generating short-term wins by showing measurable improvement from a limited pilot project; this classification identifies the early change step that challenges complacency and establishes a reason for action.

Creating urgency by demonstrating why maintaining the current permit process is unacceptable; this classification identifies the early change step that challenges complacency and establishes a reason for action.

Anchoring change by embedding the portal in recruitment, training, and organizational culture; this classification identifies the early change step that challenges complacency and establishes a reason for action.
questions.x: Using data and complaints to show the current situation is unacceptable = creating a sense of urgency (Kotter step 1).

questions.q: Which part of the case most clearly represents Kotter’s guiding coalition?
o: The measured reduction in processing time produced by the pilot in one district; this interpretation identifies the group responsible for coordinating influence, expertise, and support during change.

The online portal used by residents to submit documents and monitor permit progress; this interpretation identifies the group responsible for coordinating influence, expertise, and support during change.

The group of employees, specialists, residents, and IT staff are owners of the change; this interpretation identifies the group responsible for coordinating influence, expertise, and support during change

The waiting-time information and citizen complaints presented by the department head; this interpretation identifies the group responsible for coordinating influence, expertise, and support during change.

The national accessibility standards that will become mandatory for municipal digital services; this interpretation identifies the group responsible for coordinating influence, expertise, and support during change.

The vision describing accessible permit services with continuing human support when required; this interpretation identifies the group responsible for coordinating influence, expertise, and support during change.
questions.x: The mixed group of employees, specialists, residents and IT staff that owns and steers the change = the guiding coalition.

questions.q: Which case result should be classified as a short-term win supporting the change?
o: The guiding group's inclusion of residents, specialists, employees, and information-technology staff; this classification connects visible early progress with stronger credibility and continued support for implementation.

Employees' concern that their administrative experience may become less valuable after digitization; this classification connects visible early progress with stronger credibility and continued support for implementation.

The pilot's measurable 30 percent reduction in processing time within one district; this classification connects visible early progress with stronger credibility and continued support for implementation.

The future legal requirement to meet national standards for accessible digital public services; this classification connects visible early progress with stronger credibility and continued support for implementation.

The long-term vision of accessible permits with continuing human assistance when residents need it; this classification connects visible early progress with stronger credibility and continued support for implementation.

The department's history of using paper files and offering appointments at municipal offices; this classification connects visible early progress with stronger credibility and continued support for implementation.
questions.x: A measurable, visible early result (30% faster in one district) = a short-term win.

questions.q: Which function of management focuses on defining goals and determining how to achieve them?
o: Organizing
Planning
Leading
Controlling
questions.x: Planning = setting goals and deciding how to reach them.

questions.q: Which contemporary trends are most shaping management nowadays?
o: Elimination of technology
Decline of globalization
Decrease in innovation
Focus on diversity and sustainability
questions.x: The course names diversity (DEI) and sustainability as the trends shaping management today.

questions.q: A manager redesigns the department by grouping related tasks and assigning responsibility for each group to a team leader. Which management function does this best illustrate?
o: Forecasting
Leading
Controlling
Organizing
questions.x: Grouping tasks and assigning responsibility = designing structure, so organizing.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the view that management is “the art of getting things done through the efforts of other people”?
o: Managers achieve objectives by coordinating and supporting the work of others.
Managers contribute mainly by creating formal rules and procedures.
Managers should personally complete the organization's most important tasks.
Managers are responsible only for measuring employee performance.
questions.x: Management = reaching goals through other people, so coordinating and supporting their work.

questions.q: What are the three critical skills identified by Robert Katz for successful leaders?
o: Management, Communication, and Organizational skills
Technical, Interpersonal, and Conceptual skills
Strategic, Tactical, and Operational skills
Analytical, Emotional, and Practical skills
questions.x: Katz: technical, interpersonal (human) and conceptual skills.

questions.q: An employee who has positive feelings towards their job, is exhibiting:
o: Introversion
Conscientiousness
Agreeableness
Job satisfaction
questions.x: Positive feelings toward your job = job satisfaction (a work attitude).

questions.q: Which is a key job attitude at work?
o: Personality
Job satisfaction
Charisma
Job characteristics
questions.x: The two key work attitudes are job satisfaction and organizational commitment. Personality and charisma are traits; job characteristics are causes of attitudes.

questions.q: What does an attitude refer to?
o: A learned ability to perform a task
Our pay and benefits
Our opinions, beliefs, and feelings about our environment
A plan we make
questions.x: An attitude = our opinions, beliefs and feelings about aspects of our environment.

questions.q: What is organizational commitment?
o: Our pay level
A job task list
Emotional attachment to the company
Compliance with organizational rules and policies
questions.x: Organizational commitment = the emotional attachment people have to the company they work for.

questions.q: Which decision type sets the organization’s course?
o: Strategic
Tactical
Programmed
Operational
questions.x: Strategic decisions set the organization's long-term course; tactical and operational decisions implement it.

questions.q: A restaurant automatically reorders a standard quantity of ingredients whenever inventory reaches a predetermined level. What type of decision is this?
o: Creative decision
Programmed decision
Nonprogrammed decision
Strategic decision
questions.x: A routine, recurring decision handled by a fixed rule = programmed decision.

questions.q: Which is a barrier to effective communication?
o: Lack of attention
Information overload
Noise in the environment
Receiver
questions.x: Information overload is a communication barrier. Noise and the receiver are components of the process model.

questions.q: Which decision-making model aims for a “satisfactory” outcome?
o: Rational
Creative
Intuitive
Bounded rationality
questions.x: Bounded rationality leads to satisficing: choosing the first alternative that meets your minimum criteria.

questions.q: Which is a nonverbal communication cue?
o: Text
Phone call
Memo
Facial expressions
questions.x: Facial expressions are nonverbal. Memos, texts and phone calls use words (verbal or written).

questions.q: During a management meeting, members with doubts remain silent because they want to preserve agreement with the dominant majority. Which problem is the group experiencing?
o: Groupthink
Social facilitation
Brainstorming
Cognitive diversity
questions.x: Staying silent to keep group harmony = groupthink.

questions.q: Two employees heard the same announcement. One interprets it as an opportunity, while the other interprets it as a threat because of previous experiences. Which communication barrier best explains the difference?
o: Upward communication
Formalization
Channel expansion
Selective perception
questions.x: Interpreting the same message differently because of your own experiences and expectations = selective perception.

questions.q: What is a goal?
o: A time-based measurable action
An outcome statement of what to accomplish
A company's mission statement
A detailed strategy plan
questions.x: A goal is an outcome statement of what you want to accomplish. An objective is the precise, time-based, measurable action.

questions.q: Which goal best satisfies the SMART criteria?
o: Become the industry's most respected company.
Reduce average customer waiting time from eight to five minutes by 30 June.
Improve customer service significantly.
Encourage employees to respond to customers more quickly.
questions.x: Only this goal is specific, measurable (8 → 5 minutes) and time-bound (by 30 June).

questions.q: What is an objective?
o: A long-term goal that defines direction of the organization
A general outcome statement
A broad vision of success
A precise, time-based, measurable action
questions.x: An objective is precise, time-based and measurable. The broad outcome statement is a goal.

questions.q: What does Management by Objectives (MBO) aim to do?
o: Align subordinate objectives with overall goals
Translate mission into measures
Define the company mission and vision
Report on social and environmental results
questions.x: MBO (Drucker) aligns employees' objectives with the organization's overall goals.

questions.q: What is a goal?
o: An outcome statement of what to accomplish
A time-based measurable action
A detailed strategy plan
A company's mission statement
questions.x: A goal is an outcome statement of what you want to accomplish. An objective is the precise, time-based, measurable action.

questions.q: According to Herzberg’s two-factor theory, which action is most likely to increase motivation by providing a motivator rather than merely improving a hygiene factor?
o: Improving the office temperature
Clarifying the company's administrative policies
Giving employees meaningful responsibility for complete projects
Increasing job security
questions.x: Meaningful responsibility is a motivator. Policies, office temperature and job security are hygiene factors.

questions.q: In a strongly collectivist culture, which managerial practice is most likely to be effective?
o: Assigning work without considering group membership
Emphasizing only individual competition and personal recognition
Connecting rewards and goals to the performance of the group
Avoiding long-term relationships among team members
questions.x: Collectivist cultures put the group first, so tie rewards and goals to group performance.

questions.q: What is “power distance” in Hofstede’s model?
o: Acceptance of power and authority differences
Focus on risk and uncertainty
Value of work and earnings
Preference for collective interests over individual ones
questions.x: Power distance = how much people accept unequal distribution of power and authority.

questions.q: A culture emphasizes persistence, future rewards, and future investment rather than immediate results. Which Hofstede dimension does this describe?
o: Masculinity
Power distance
Long-term orientation
Individualism
questions.x: Persistence and future rewards over immediate results = long-term orientation.

questions.q: A national culture strongly values cooperation, quality of life, and concern for others rather than competition and visible achievement. In Hofstede’s framework, this culture is relatively:
o: Masculine
Feminine
High in power distance
High in uncertainty avoidance
questions.x: Valuing cooperation and quality of life over competition and achievement = a feminine culture (low masculinity).

questions.q: A financial-services company faces new regulations concerning artificial intelligence and growing customer concern about automated decisions. A manager with extensive AI knowledge explains the technical risks to senior leaders and consults employees who will use the systems before recommending procedural changes. Which pair of leadership concepts is demonstrated by the manager?
o: Expert power and people-oriented leadership based on knowledge and consultation
Legitimate power and task-oriented leadership based on position and deadlines
Reward power and laissez-faire leadership based on incentives and employee independence
Referent power and democratic leadership based on admiration and formal voting
questions.x: Influence from AI knowledge = expert power. Consulting the employees who will use the systems = people-oriented.

questions.q: Severe flooding interrupts a company’s main supply route. The logistics director has formal authority to activate an emergency sourcing plan. She also relies on a climate-risk specialist whose knowledge helps the company evaluate more resilient and sustainable suppliers. Which pair correctly identifies the sources of power in the case?
o: Reward power from the director and referent power from the specialist
Referent power from the director and coercive power from the specialist
Expert power from the director and legitimate power from the specialist
Legitimate power from the director and expert power from the specialist
questions.x: Formal authority = legitimate power (director). Specialist knowledge = expert power (specialist).

questions.q: A manufacturer is replacing a polluting production process with cleaner technology. The operations director defines conversion targets, assigns responsibilities, and monitors deadlines. She also invites employees from different backgrounds and job levels to discuss how the change may affect them and adapt the training accordingly. Which description best summarizes the director’s leadership behavior?
o: Task-oriented and autocratic leadership emphasizing targets and centralized managerial control
People-oriented and democratic leadership emphasizing consultation without formal performance targets
Laissez-faire and people-oriented leadership allowing employees to direct implementation independently
Task-oriented and people-oriented leadership balancing targets with employee inclusion
questions.x: Targets, responsibilities and deadlines = task-oriented. Inviting employees and adapting training = people-oriented. She does both.

questions.q: A cybersecurity specialist influences an executive team because of her knowledge and experience, although she has no formal managerial position. Which source of power explains her influence?
o: Coercive power
Expert power
Reward power
Legitimate power
questions.x: Influence from knowledge and experience without a formal position = expert power.

questions.q: A nonprofit director learns that employees performing comparable work are paid differently across gender and ethnic groups. She openly acknowledges the problem, publishes the review method, corrects the pay gaps, and asks employees what support they need for future development. She accepts personal responsibility for maintaining fair practices. Which description best explains the director’s leadership styles?
o: Charismatic and transformational leadership connecting personal influence with an inspiring vision
Authentic and servant leadership combining transparency for employees
Values-based and autocratic leadership combining organizational principles with centralized decisions
Transactional and ethical leadership linking fair treatment mainly to performance rewards
questions.x: Openly acknowledging the problem and taking responsibility = authentic. Asking what employees need to develop = servant leadership.

questions.q: New international regulations require companies to explain automated hiring decisions. Public concern about discrimination is also increasing. A technology leader commissions independent bias audits, publishes the results, and sets a strategic goal to develop transparent and inclusive AI products. Which interpretation best explains the company’s leadership response?
o: Servant leadership develops employees while leaving the automated system strategically unchanged
Authentic and charismatic leadership emphasizes personal identity and persuasive public communication
Ethical and transformational leadership connects transparency with inclusive strategic innovation
Transactional leadership maintains existing products through rewards linked to regulatory compliance
questions.x: Independent audits and publishing results = ethical. A strategic goal for transparent, inclusive innovation = transformational.

questions.q: A fashion retailer discovers that a low-cost supplier has unsafe working conditions and causes serious environmental damage. The CEO ends the contract despite the short-term cost. She communicates a vision of a fair, low-carbon supply chain and invites employees to redesign sourcing practices. Which description best explains the CEO’s leadership response?
o: Transactional and servant leadership linking supplier decisions to rewards and employee development
Authentic and laissez-faire leadership expressing personal values while limiting organizational direction
Charismatic and transactional leadership using personal influence and performance-based exchanges
Ethical and transformational leadership protecting stakeholders while communicating a new vision
questions.x: Ending the contract to protect workers and the environment = ethical. A new vision plus involving employees = transformational.

questions.q: New equality legislation strengthens protection for gender identity and sexual orientation. At the same time, qualified applicants increasingly expect remote and flexible work. A consulting company revises its inclusion policies, trains managers, and creates virtual teams that recruit talent from a wider geographic area. Which interpretation best explains the company’s organizational response?
o: Economic pressures encourage divisional structures and standardized recruitment across all locations
Legal and sociocultural pressures encourage inclusive policies and geographically flexible virtual structures
Technological pressures encourage matrix structures and specialist recruitment within one location
Internal workforce pressures encourage functional structures and locally restricted recruitment practices
questions.x: New law = legal pressure; applicants expecting remote work = sociocultural. The response: inclusive policies and virtual teams.

questions.q: Growing demand for reusable products leads a furniture company to collaborate with repair businesses, recycling firms, and design startups. Teams from these organizations share knowledge and coordinate activities without being placed inside one traditional hierarchy. Which interpretation best describes the company’s strategic response?
o: A geographic structure supports regional independence in response to changing national regulations
A networked structure supports external collaboration in response to the circular-economy trend
A divisional structure supports product independence in response to changing customer segments
A functional structure supports internal specialization in response to changing professional standards
questions.x: Collaborating with outside firms without one hierarchy = network (virtual) structure, responding to the circular-economy trend.

questions.q: A company displays diversity statements throughout its offices and lists inclusion as a core value. However, managers repeatedly promote employees who share the same background and dismiss reports of biased behavior. Employees conclude that the organization’s actual priorities differ from its public message. Which cultural levels are represented by the statements and promotion patterns?
o: External environmental forces in the statements, with espoused values in repeated decisions
Underlying assumptions in the statements, with visible artifacts in repeated decisions
Artifacts and espoused values in the statements, with underlying assumptions in repeated decisions
Organizational structures in the statements, with external pressures in repeated decisions
questions.x: Displayed statements are artifacts and espoused values. What managers repeatedly do reveals the real underlying assumptions.

questions.q: A newly diverse project team initially experiences disagreement about priorities and communication styles. Instead of removing members who disagree, the leader helps the team establish decision rules, clarify roles, and develop norms that ensure every member can contribute. Trust and cohesion begin to increase. Which two team-development stages are represented in sequence?
o: Performing followed by adjourning as initial conflict gives way to role clarification
Norming followed by performing as shared expectations give way to initial conflict
Forming followed by storming as members first meet and then avoid disagreement
Storming followed by norming as disagreement gives way to shared expectations
questions.x: Disagreement about priorities = storming. Agreeing on rules, roles and norms = norming.

questions.q: A shift toward hybrid work leads a company to add remote specialists from several countries to an established product team. The team leader notices uncertainty about roles, technology, and meeting expectations. She schedules orientation sessions and helps members rebuild shared working agreements. Which two team-development stages best match the change described?
o: Forming after adding members, followed by norming as shared agreements develop
Performing after adding members, followed by storming as role expectations become clear
Norming after adding members, followed by adjourning after agreements are established
Storming after adding members, followed by performing after the first orientation session
questions.x: New members restart the team at forming (uncertainty about roles); rebuilding shared working agreements = norming.

questions.q: A travel company plans sustainable services for a rapidly growing international market. Its project team includes members with different cultural backgrounds and professional expertise. The team also consults local community leaders, environmental experts, and industry partners to understand emerging expectations and opportunities. Which interpretation best explains the factors strengthening the response?
o: Centralized expertise broadens international insight, while closed networking identifies future partnership opportunities
Cultural similarity broadens sustainability insight, while personal networking identifies future regulatory developments
Professional similarity broadens customer insight, while operational networking identifies future market developments
Team diversity broadens market insight, while strategic networking identifies future trends and opportunities
questions.x: Diverse members broaden insight; consulting outside leaders and experts about future trends = strategic networking.

questions.q: How should the regional managers’ successful monthly packages be classified relative to the original discount plan?
o: A functional strategy because the packages concern only maintenance procedures within individual hotel buildings; this classification distinguishes management's original plan from the pattern produced through organizational learning.

A mission statement because the packages redefine the organization's enduring purpose and stakeholders; this classification distinguishes management's original plan from the pattern produced through organizational learning.

An intended strategy because the packages were the original approach approved before local testing; this classification distinguishes management's original plan from the pattern produced through organizational learning.

A realized strategy because local experiments produced a different successful pattern of action; this classification distinguishes management's original plan from the pattern produced through organizational learning.

A corporate strategy because the packages automatically move UrbanStay into an unrelated industry; this classification distinguishes management's original plan from the pattern produced through organizational learning.

A stakeholder analysis because the packages classify remote professionals by power and organizational interest; this classification distinguishes management's original plan from the pattern produced through organizational learning
questions.x: The successful pattern that emerged locally and replaced the plan = realized strategy.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, growing demand for extended work-from-anywhere stays is classified as what?
o: A weakness because it is an internal limitation reducing the efficiency of hotel operations; this interpretation separates an external growth possibility from internal capabilities and environmental risks.
An opportunity because it is an external trend that UrbanStay can use for growth; this interpretation separates an external growth possibility from internal capabilities and environmental risks.

A core competence because it is a coordinated organizational capability that competitors cannot copy; this interpretation separates an external growth possibility from internal capabilities and environmental risks

A strength because it is an internal capability already controlled and protected by UrbanStay; this interpretation separates an external growth possibility from internal capabilities and environmental risks.

A value-chain activity because it is a process performed directly within UrbanStay's operations; this interpretation separates an external growth possibility from internal capabilities and environmental risks.

A threat because it is an external development that necessarily reduces demand for accommodation; this interpretation separates an external growth possibility from internal capabilities and environmental risks.
questions.x: An external trend the company can use for growth = opportunity.

questions.q: Which revised vision best describes an aspirational future for UrbanStay?
o: UrbanStay operates hotels in business districts and maintains relationships with corporate travel departments; this wording distinguishes a desired future position from present purpose, activities, and compliance responsibilities.

UrbanStay aims to become Europe's leading home for flexible and sustainable mobile professionals; this wording distinguishes a desired future position from present purpose, activities, and compliance responsibilities.

UrbanStay provides dependable rooms and workspaces to current business and leisure travelers; this wording distinguishes a desired future position from present purpose, activities, and compliance responsibilities.

UrbanStay follows legal standards for safety, employment, data protection, and environmental reporting; this wording distinguishes a desired future position from present purpose, activities, and compliance responsibilities.

UrbanStay renovates meeting rooms, monitors energy use, and develops monthly accommodation packages; this wording distinguishes a desired future position from present purpose, activities, and compliance responsibilities.

UrbanStay serves guests who currently require accommodation, workspaces, and local community activities; this wording distinguishes a desired future position from present purpose, activities, and compliance responsibilities.
questions.x: A vision is aspirational and about the future: 'aims to become Europe's leading home…'. The others describe present activities or compliance.

questions.q: In Schein’s model, the belief that paper records are inherently safer is best classified as what?
o: An espoused strategy because the belief is the hospital's formally published competitive plan; this interpretation locates the belief at the appropriate level of Schein's organizational culture model.
An underlying assumption because the belief is deeply taken for granted by experienced staff; this interpretation locates the belief at the appropriate level of Schein's organizational culture model

A visible artifact because the belief is a physical and directly observable feature of the hospital; this interpretation locates the belief at the appropriate level of Schein's organizational culture model.

A short-term win because the belief provides measurable evidence that the change is succeeding; this interpretation locates the belief at the appropriate level of Schein's organizational culture model.

A functional structure because the belief determines how specialist departments report to management; this interpretation locates the belief at the appropriate level of Schein's organizational culture model.
questions.x: A deeply taken-for-granted belief = underlying assumption, the deepest level of culture.

questions.q: Which action most clearly represents Lewin’s refreezing stage?
o: Embedding electronic documentation in job descriptions, audits, and performance reviews; this classification identifies how new behavior becomes stabilized through formal systems, expectations, and routines

Providing initial training while employees are still learning the unfamiliar electronic procedures; this classification identifies how new behavior becomes stabilized through formal systems, expectations, and routines.

Explaining why fragmented paper records create safety risks and unnecessary duplicated medical tests; this classification identifies how new behavior becomes stabilized through formal systems, expectations, and routines.

Comparing software suppliers before management selects the electronic system for the hospital; this classification identifies how new behavior becomes stabilized through formal systems, expectations, and routines.

Asking employees to discuss concerns before the first electronic-record pilot begins; this classification identifies how new behavior becomes stabilized through formal systems, expectations, and routines.

Testing the electronic system in one department and revising the workflow during implementation; this classification identifies how new behavior becomes stabilized through formal systems, expectations, and routines.
questions.x: Embedding the behaviour in job descriptions, audits and reviews makes it permanent = refreezing.

questions.q: How should employees who attend training but secretly continue using paper records be classified?
o: Creative participation because they formally test alternatives and share results with the implementation team; this interpretation distinguishes concealed noncompliance from open opposition, acceptance, and active commitment.

Active support because they openly encourage colleagues to use the electronic system consistently; this interpretation distinguishes concealed noncompliance from open opposition, acceptance, and active commitment.

Passive resistance because they appear compliant but privately continue the previous behavior; this interpretation distinguishes concealed noncompliance from open opposition, acceptance, and active commitment

Enthusiastic adoption because they use the system beyond the minimum expectations of their roles; this interpretation distinguishes concealed noncompliance from open opposition, acceptance, and active commitment.

Commitment because they personally invest additional effort in making the new workflow successful; this interpretation distinguishes concealed noncompliance from open opposition, acceptance, and active commitment.

Active resistance because they organize visible protests and publicly reject management's authority; this interpretation distinguishes concealed noncompliance from open opposition, acceptance, and active commitment.
questions.x: Looking compliant while quietly keeping the old behaviour = passive resistance.

Strategic decision

An outcome statement of what to accomplish

questions.q: A company enters a foreign market by creating a new business that it owns together with a local company. Which global expansion strategy is this?

Wholly owned subsidiary
Exporting
Joint venture
questions.x: A new business owned together with a local firm = joint venture.

questions.q: What does GLOBE stand for?
o: Global Leadership and Organizational Business Environment
Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness
Global Learning and Organizational Behavior Evaluation
Global Leadership and Operations Benchmarking Exercise

questions.q: Employees willingly support a team leader because they admire and identify with him. Which source of power is primarily illustrated?

Reward power
Referent power
Coercive power

Expert power from the director and legitimate power from the specialist
